proposedOverrides.name: Alabama people
proposedOverrides.summary: The Alabama are an Indigenous people whose earlier homes lay in what is now Alabama. Communities later established homes farther west; the Alabama-Coushatta Tribe of Texas preserves a shared political history with the closely associated Coushatta people.

overrideClaims.text: The Alabama are an Indigenous people whose earlier homes lay in what is now Alabama. Communities later established homes farther west; the Alabama-Coushatta Tribe of Texas preserves a shared political history with the closely associated Coushatta people.

overrideClaims.reason: Replace the imported modern U.S. state summary with the Indigenous identity appropriate to a 1530 to 1783 Alabama River polygon.

scopeNotes: The imported polygon lies around the Alabama River and covers 1530 to 1783. It is not the modern U.S. state. Neither its boundary nor its starting year is verified by this narrative.

The modern Texas tribe includes Alabama and Coushatta histories; the card preserves affiliations of named people and institutions. A Louisiana Coushatta artist living with Alabama-Coushatta family is explicitly identified.

The tribal chief history calls the languages mutually understandable, while the dictionary authors explain that they are distinct and mutual comprehension is limited without learning the other language. The card follows the specialist linguistic account and records the disagreement here.
Migration dates vary by community and source. No single crossing date or universal route is asserted. The French departure does not mean that all Alabama towns ceased immediately.
The tribal history, Briscoe finding aid and encyclopedia give different reservation acreage figures. No acreage is asserted. The finding aid was read, not the original deeds.
Smither’s 1932 article is used for attributed discussion of the 1831 census and household livelihoods. Its colonial stereotypes, casualty counts and racial descriptions are not reproduced.
The Gorman catalog does not supply basket materials, technique or a making narrative. These are not invented. The 1973 date is manufacture; the accession number is not used as that date.
The dictionary introduction and alphabet page are one work for source budgeting. Quoted vocabulary totals four words.

Public Law 100-89 Title II sections 201 to 204 support historical recognition changes. The unrelated Ysleta del Sur provisions are not applied to Alabama-Coushatta, and no current gaming-law advice is supplied.
The Oklahoma tribal history has an erroneous 1888 Dawes Act date, which is not reproduced. Independent historical review, geometry assessment and depth certification remain pending.
